speakeroldname: Hon. R. J. MANION (Minister of Railways) :
speechtext: Before the question is put I should like to show the disadvantage of the proposal put forward in the amendment. The proposal is, as I understand it, that the salaries of the trustees be paid directly by parliament rather than by the railway. In the first place this would make a very radical change in the whole system of management and operation of the Canadian National Railways, and I do not think my hon. friend has given it the serious consideration which he devotes to other subjects; had he done so, he would probably not have moved the amendment. First of all, while this would not be a reflection in any way upon the trustees, it would nevertheless convert them from trustees of the Canadian National railways into virtual civil servants. It would bring them distinctly under the control of the parliament of Canada. They would be placed in this position, that if the government of the day, whatever government might be in power, so chose, it could use the fact that it was going to have to vote the salaries of these trustees for the purpose of getting rid of them forthwith. Moreover, it would place in the hands of any individual member of the house a club which he could use over the trustees if he were so inclined. In other words, if some hon. member wanted to have a station built at-
Riviere du Loup.

Someone suggests, a station at Riviere du Loup. Well, if an hon. member wanted a station there or anywhere else he might, if he were persistent enough, go to one of the trustees and give him to understand that if he did not agree to the building of this station, or it might be the building of a branch line, or the performance of some other act on the part of the national railways, it was his intention to oppose most strenuously, and to get his friends to oppose in the house, the payment of salary. I think it would be a most retrograde step so far as the Canadian National Railways are concerned-the most retrograde step ever 'taken by any government in Canada. It would be throwing the national railways into the political arena to an extent such as they never have been under any government at any time in the history of our railways.

The minister seems to find some objection to placing the trustees under the control of parliament, but that is where they should be, and that is where we differ from the hon. gentleman. There is a very radical difference of opinion between us. As to the argument that this might constitute a club which might be held over the heads of the trustees, all I have to say is this, that if they are the men we expect they will be they will not be afraid of any such club. The same argument might apply to any deputy minister. What is to prevent any member of parliament from saying to a deputy minister that he will oppose a vote for his salary unless the deputy builds him a wharf or arranges to provide a post office? The situation is exactly the same, but so far as I know, no such attempt has ever been made by any member of parliament. I only wish to repeat the argument advanced last night, namely, that these men constitute a new body, a new species of control. They are not directors, we have been told; they cannot like ordinary directors be removed by the shareholders at the end of the year. They are not trustees in the sense of an ordinary trustee in bankruptcy, because they are not under the control of any court. They are not obliged to consult anyone. We simply hand over to three men to whom we pay a salary the whole management and control of the greatest asset which the Canadian people have.

I do not agree that they
are receivers in bankruptcy or anything of the kind. At any rate, it seems to me that if you attempted to place them on that basis you would find it very difficult 'to obtain good men to undertake the duties. I do not think the position of trustee is akin to that of a deputy minister, because it has never been the custom of this or of any other government, or of the parliament of Canada, to pay

I submit, as I did last night, that by the submission of the railway budget to the Minister of Finance and the necessity of voting the financial needs of the railway in this house, the railway will quite adequately be under the control of parliament. I do not wish to delay the motion at all, but certainly I do not think it would be wise for parliament to take any such step as that contemplated by the amendment.

If I mistake not, my hon. friend from Quebec South (Mr. Power) and my hon. friend from North Waterloo (Mr. Euler) strongly supported that principle, and I do not think that to-day we should take this retrograde step. But my more immediate purpose in rising at this time is to raise a point of order as to the validity of the amendment. I submit, Mr. Chairman, that this amendment is out of order because it interferes with the destination of supply and could not be raised at this time in this manner.	;

I want to make a suggestion not only to the minister but to the government as a whole, and especially to the Prime Minister, in order that the discussion of this bill in committee may take up the least possible time. What is the history of this legislation? Section 5 of the bill is based on the report of the Duff commission, a resume of which I have here, and in article 203 on page 63 I read:
Three trustees should he appointed by the governor in council, in whom should be vested all the powers of the present board of directors of the Canadian National Railways, both in respect of the parent and all subsidiary corporations of the system; and any and every power and authority necessary to enable them to administer the property and operate the system and every part thereof.
Senators and members of the House of Commons and persons bolding or having within five years held office or place of profit under the crown in the right of the dominion or one of the provinces of Canada, should be disqualified for appointment.
There have been three drafts of the bill which we are now studying. The first draft was introduced and read a first time in the Senate on October 27, 1932, and section 4 of that draft reads as follows:
(1)	No person who is a senator or member of the House of Commons, and no person holding or having within five years held any office or position to which any salary is attached payable directly or indirectly by His Majesty, in the right of the Dominion of Canada, or of any of the provinces thereof, shall be eligible for appointment as trustee.
(2)	Vacancies among the trustees arising from any reason shall be filled from time to time by the governor in council from a list of eight persons then named by the remaining trustees or trustee. All trustees shall be eligible for reappointment if so listed.

C.N.R.-C.P.R. Bill
This section in the first draft bill which was read a first time in the Senate on October 27 is in accordance with section 203 of the report of the commissioners.
The bill was redrafted by order of the Senate committee on railways, telegraphs and harbours, and dn that redraft, section 5 corresponds to section 203 of the report of the commissioners, including that eminent man, as he was described by the Prime Minister yesterday, Sir Joseph Flavelle. Section 5 in this redrafted bill reads as follows:
No person shall be eligible for appointment who at the time of any proposed appointment of a trustee or trustees under this act is, or within five years immediately then preceding has been,-
(a) a member of the Senate of Canada;
(b) a member of the House of Commons of Canada;	_
(c)	a member of the council of any province of Canada;
(d)	a candidate nominated under any act of the dominion or of any province of Canada for election as a member of the House of Commons of Canada or of the legislative assembly of any province of Canada; or
(e)	the holder of any office, place or appointment to which is, or while it was held by him was, attached any salary payable directly by His Majesty in his right of the Dominion of Canada.
That section in the second draft of the bill is in conformity with the previous quotations which I have given.
Now I come to section 5 in the bill before us, which reads:
The trustees shall be paid by the National company such salaries as may from time to time be fixed by the governor in council, and if any trustee is in receipt of a pension from any railway company he shall not be entitled to receive or to be paid such pension during his term of office.
(2) Each trustee shall be paid but one salary, and saving and excepting that and his right to prepayment or repayment of his proper expenditures made while engaged in and upon the affairs of National Railways, he shall not be entitled upon any ground to any recompense or emolument.
The third draft bill which was passed by the Senate on February 23 last is entirely different from the other draft. I remember that my hon. friend from York-Sunbury protested in the house against the alteration of the first two drafts, and he protested also against the report of the commissioners because the first and second drafts were in accordance with their report. My first observation with regard to this is that the Senate has been putting aside the suggestions made by the commissioners, and suggestions which were approved by the Senate in the first and second instance. The Senate has modified the views expressed by the commissioners, and 53719-257
has not accepted them. If the Senate had not accepted these proposals in regard to the qualifications of the trustees, why does the government stand so stubbornly behind the appointment of only three trustees? In the Bible there is a book entitled Numbers. It would seem that the government attaches very great importance to the number three. In my view there should be more than three trustees.
Since the government puts aside the views expressed by the commissioners with regard to the appointment of the trustees, why is it that we should consider their view so sacred when it applies to other matters? No one is bound to accept those views; we have to weigh the pros and cons, and decide accordingly. May I make another practical suggestion to the government? Until now the Minister of Railways has been doing very well; I congratulate him. He has no legal training, but he has sound judgment. That is the difference between him and his leader. In his dealings with the committee he has shown good judgment. I pay him no small compliment, because I place him above a superman. It is a great compliment, and he deserves it.
It is essential that the house should know each step which has been taken since the report was made by the commissioners. That report is the basis for the legislation we are now studying. As undoubtedly the minister, although not a lawyer, has much better legal sense than has the Prime Minister, why does he not explain the legislation from the time the commissioners made their report? Why does he not explain every amendment made by the Senate both in committee and in the Senate chamber? It seems to me by doing so he would prevent much useless talk, and the discussion would be centred on the vital parts of the legislation. I have no officers at my disposal, and any information I have obtained I had to get myself, because I like to study conscientiously every piece of legislation brought before the house. What I say now I say not for the benefit of the Minister of Railways but mostly for the benefit of the right hon. leader of the government. If he were the junior clerk in my country law office I would say to him, "Mark you, my boy, you should listen to this wise advice; it is never too late for you to listen to something. You are like the Bourbons, you have learned nothing and forgotten nothing. It is time for you to forget what you do not know, and to learn what you should know." That is what I would most humbly and respectfully say to the gentleman who honours us by his absence. I hope some good friend will report to him what I have said about him. But I

do not wish to be discourteous to the Minister of Railways, because he is a gentleman. He has polite manners, and deserves to be treated fairly and squarely. I offer these suggestions to the house, and when they are accepted the minister will find that the legislation will pass much more quickly.

I should like to move an amendment to this subsection. At present it reads as follows:
6. The governor in council may from time to time appoint or reappoint a trustee to fill any vacancy among the trustees from any cause occurring. The appointee shall be selected from a panel of eight names to be provided by a nominating board composed of the president of the Exchequer Court of Canada, the chief commissioner of the Board of Railway Commissioners for Canada and the existing or remaining trustees. Such board shall be convened by the chairman of the trustees. In the case of an imminent vacancy the board may convene and act in anticipation thereof. If no such panel is so provided within ten days after the occurrence of a vacancy the governor in council may appoint as he may be advised.
I propose to move:
That all the words after the word "occurring" in the third line be stricken out.
The point I wish to make is-
What is all this about? What is the amendment? Read it.

I have just read it. It would seem to me that the amendment has something to do with Bill A of the Senate. I do not know just how far the hon. member has proceeded in his Study of the bill, but I may tell him that is the bill we are now discussing. Further, we have been doing it for some few days.
Would you mind telling us what you are discussing? Nobody knows what you are talking about.
Well, that is too bad.
I mean that the hon. member is not speaking distinctly. He is speaking down into his book, and hon. members on this side of the house cannot hear him.
Could you hear if he were looking at the ceiling?

That is probably the first time since I came into this house I have been told I did not make enough row. In order to please the hon. member from Toronto I will raise my voice a little. The amendment I am proposing is that all the words after the word "occurring" in the third line of subsection 1 of section 6 be stricken out. I propose that amendment because I believe the selection of persons to fill vacancies should be made in the same manner as the selection of the original trustees. There is no reason why in the selection of trustees two systems should operate. The present provision in that regard will serve only to perpetuate the members of the board originally selected, if they desire to be perpetuated. It will have the effect of forming a sort of small family compact controlling the Canadian National Railways. The discussion on this amendment would be along the 'line of that which has taken place since the beginning of the debate. If it is found impossible to place the trustees under the control of parliament, at least I believe they should be under the control of a government responsible to parliament and to the people. Therefore, as soon as I have drafted the resolution I shall move that that part of the section dealing with the composition or creation of a panel shall be stricken from this subsection. The amendment about which I have been speaking I have now prepared, and shall hand to the clerk.

On section 7-Removal from office or reduction of salary.

I have
an amendment to move. To my mind section 7 is the most vital section in the whole legislation, and there are two possible amendments that could be moved; either delete the section entirely, which would leave the removal from office of the trustees under the jurisdiction of the governor in council; or strike out the words "Senate and" which would leave the control with the House of Commons as distinct from both houses.
This section comprises in itself the features to which I mainly object in this legislation. That is it means complete abrogation and abdication of government control over these trustees. There is no control whatever over their removal or dismissal. The entire national railways of Canada are to be put in the control of three trustees and this House of Commons has not the slightest power over their removal. As pointed out last night by the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power) in regard to salary, they shall not suffer any reduction in salary unless for assigned cause and on address of the Senate and the House of Commons. I interpret that to mean that if any one of the trustees objects to any reduction of salary that would bind all the trustees, and it could not be done except on address of both houses. I am aware that there is a similar provision in regard to judges and in regard to the auditor general, also I think in regard to the chief electoral officer, 53719-257$
but I submit that the argument submitted by the Prime Minister in regard to judges cannot apply to these trustees. H we pass this section we are certainly forfeiting in perpetuity the control by this house of these trustees. Under other sections of the act they are a self-perpetuating body and under this section this House of Commons forfeits all control and ownership of our national railway. I do not think I can serve any useful purpose by elaborating the stand we have taken on this side of the house; it was emphasized on the second reading. But to my -mind this section is the most objectionable of the whole legislation.
It is moved by Mr. Mackenzie (Vancouver) to amend section 7 by deleting the section entirely. I submit that this amendment is out of order.
Why?
I move to substitute number 8 for number 7 and to leave out all the words after the figure 7.

To avoid unnecessary complication and delay may I suggest that I shall be glad to have section 7 also stand.
